entities.summary:
The neutron star, an ultra-dense celestial object formed from the collapsed core of a massive star, represents one of the most extreme states of matter known, profoundly reshaping humanity's understanding of stellar evolution and fundamental physics. First theorized in the 1930s by pioneering physicists like Lev Landau, Walter Baade, and Fritz Zwicky, its existence was considered speculative until the accidental discovery of pulsars in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish at Cambridge University. This breakthrough validated a half-century of theoretical work, confirming the universe harbored objects where gravity compresses matter to densities unimaginable on Earth, a teaspoon of which would weigh billions of tons. Neutron stars, with their immense gravitational fields and rapid rotation, act as cosmic laboratories, challenging and expanding the boundaries of general relativity and quantum mechanics.

Formed during Type II supernovae, when stars significantly more massive than the Sun exhaust their nuclear fuel and undergo catastrophic gravitational collapse, neutron stars are typically only 20 kilometers in diameter yet possess a mass comparable to the Sun. Their structure includes a solid crust, a superfluid interior, and an exotic core where the behavior of matter under extreme pressure and temperature remains an active area of research. Many neutron stars are observed as pulsars, emitting highly regular beams of electromagnetic radiation that sweep across Earth, creating a 'lighthouse effect' detected by radio telescopes. The stability and precision of these pulses are so exact that they rival atomic clocks, providing unique tools for probing interstellar medium and testing gravitational theories.
